Health Information Bill Second Reading debate Second Reading12 January 2026 bill-773, bill-774, bill-775

A Second Reading debate on the Health Information Bill, which requires licensed healthcare providers and retail pharmacies to contribute key health information to the National Electronic Health Record and sets rules for access, sharing and safeguards.

The Bill requires all licensed healthcare providers and retail pharmacies to contribute key health information to NEHR, so a patient's records can follow them across providers. It allows patients to restrict access, while critical allergies and vaccination records remain visible, and prohibits access for employment or insurance purposes. The Minister says the Bill is intended to take effect from early 2027.

  • Mr Tan Kiat How

    • The Health Information Bill was moved for Second Reading.

      Verbatim
      The Bill be now read a Second time.

    • Singapore is ageing rapidly, with one in four Singaporeans aged 65 and above by 2030.

      Verbatim
      By 2030, one in four Singaporeans will be aged 65 and above.

    • Currently, key health records are often not accessible across providers, which can risk medication errors, delayed treatment and duplicate tests.

      Verbatim
      Such gaps can risk medication errors, delayed treatment and duplicate tests and procedures.

    • The Bill requires all licensed healthcare providers and retail pharmacies to contribute key health information to NEHR.

      Verbatim
      The HIB will require all healthcare providers licensed under the Healthcare Services Act 2020 and retail pharmacies licensed under the Health Products Act 2007 to contribute key health information about patients into NEHR.

    • Key health information includes allergies, vaccinations, diagnoses, medications, laboratory test results, radiological images and discharge summaries.

      Verbatim
      allergies, vaccinations, diagnoses, medications, laboratory test results, radiological images and discharge summaries

    • NEHR access for patient care is limited to licensed healthcare providers and their authorised individuals.

      Verbatim
      NEHR access for patient care purposes will be limited to licensed healthcare providers and their authorised individuals.

    • Accessing NEHR for employment or insurance purposes is strictly prohibited.

      Verbatim
      Accessing NEHR for purposes relating to employment or insurance will be strictly prohibited.

    • NEHR access is allowed for specified statutory medical examinations.

      Verbatim
      NEHR access will therefore be allowed for these statutory medical examinations.

    • Patients may restrict access to their NEHR information so that only select healthcare providers may have access.

      Verbatim
      they may restrict access to their NEHR information so that only select healthcare providers may have this access.

    • From the second half of this year, patients can place an Access Restriction through the HealthHub app.

      Verbatim
      From the second half of this year, patients can do so through the HealthHub app.

    • During medical emergencies, a patient's NEHR information may be accessed despite an Access Restriction, with only doctors allowed to 'break glass'.

      Verbatim
      only doctors will be allowed to "break glass".

    • Non-NEHR health information may be shared without consent only if three key criteria are met.

      Verbatim
      We will enable the scoped sharing of non-NEHR health information without an individual's consent only if three key criteria are met.

    • A first offence for unauthorised access of NEHR information under clause 38 carries a fine of up to $50,000, two years' imprisonment or both.

      Verbatim
      a person convicted of an offence relating to unauthorised access of NEHR information under clause 38 faces a fine of up to $50,000, two years’ imprisonment or both, for a first offence.

    • Healthcare providers that fail to put in place required cybersecurity or data security measures may face a fine of up to $1 million.

      Verbatim
      healthcare providers that fail to put in place the cybersecurity or data security measures required under the HIB may face a fine of up to $1 million

    • The Bill is intended to take effect from early 2027.

      Verbatim
      we intend for the Bill to take effect from early 2027.

  • Ms Mariam Jaafar

      Verbatim
      The Health Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) supports this Bill.

  • Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong

    • Dennis Tan supports the Bill but raises concerns about challenges for smaller healthcare operators such as single or dual-doctor clinics.

      Verbatim
      while I support the Bill, I wish to raise a few concerns posed by the HIB, and I will be speaking on the challenges for smaller healthcare operators, such as single or dual-doctor practitioner clinics that many of my residents rely on for their daily medical needs.

    • Dennis Tan says the $1 million cap effectively puts a ceiling on the value of the collective privacy of the nation.

      Verbatim
      the $1 million cap effectively puts a ceiling on the value of the collective privacy of the nation

  • Dr Wan Rizal

      Verbatim

Open questions from this debate (10)

Questions the debate raises that the record does not resolve. Listed as open questions, not as findings.

  • Whether the maximum fine of $1 million is sufficient to deter large healthcare organisations.
  • How MOH will ensure insurers cannot obtain NEHR-derived information through clinical notes or audit clauses.
  • What the exact funding quantum and eligibility criteria will be for small GP clinics.
  • Whether cybersecurity insurance will be offered to small providers.
  • How patients who are not digitally confident will be assisted to place or manage Access Restrictions.
  • When and whether community health partners beyond public entities will be added to the Fourth Schedule.
  • How overseas medical records will be treated in the NEHR.
  • What constitutes 'reasonable access' to NEHR for clinicians in practice.
  • How data breach notification thresholds will apply to smaller breaches.
  • Whether the list of statutory medical examinations will remain tightly scoped over time.
Public Sector (Governance) (Amendment) Bill at Second Reading Second Reading12 January 2026 bill-772

A Second Reading debate on the Public Sector (Governance) (Amendment) Bill, which would allow public agencies to share data with trusted external partners under safeguards and create related offences for misuse.

The Minister said the amendments will enable vulnerable Singaporeans to receive faster, targeted and more coordinated support, when they need it most. She also said families in need currently repeat their stories and details to many parties, and the Bill introduces criminal offences for individuals in external organisations who misuse shared data. The record does not set out commencement dates or other practical impacts beyond these stated aims.

  • Ms Jasmin Lau

    • The Bill was moved for Second Reading.

      Verbatim
      I move, “That the Bill be now read a Second time.”

    • The PSGA was introduced in 2018 to enable public agencies to share data safely and purposefully.

      Verbatim
      It helped to enable, among other objectives, public agencies to share data safely and purposefully, so that we can serve Singaporeans better.

    • The Bill provides a clear legal basis with guardrails for data sharing with trusted external partners where it serves legitimate public purposes.

      Verbatim
      It provides a clear legal basis with guardrails for data sharing with our trusted external partners, where it serves legitimate public purposes.

    • The Bill sets three safeguards: legitimate purpose, Ministerial or delegate authorisation, and contractual terms of use.

      Verbatim
      having a legitimate purpose for sharing; (b) the arrangement is specifically authorised by a Minister or the Minister's delegate; and (c) the external partner is bound by clear contractual terms of use, including data protection and security requirements.

    • The Bill does not authorise data sharing for commercial exploitation, marketing or unrelated purposes.

      Verbatim
      It does not authorise data sharing for commercial exploitation, marketing or unrelated purposes.

    • Individuals in external organisations face the same penalties as public officers for misusing shared data.

      Verbatim
      individuals in external organisations face the same level of penalties that public officers are currently subject to for misusing shared data.

    • The Bill clarifies that public agencies are permitted to use their own data to work more effectively.

      Verbatim
      public agencies are permitted to use their own data to work more effectively.

    • The PSGA and the forthcoming Health Information Bill are complementary.

      Verbatim
      Both the PSGA and the HIB are complementary Bills.

  • Mr Sharael Taha

    • The MDDI Government Parliamentary Committee and PAP MPs support the Bill.

      Verbatim
      the MPs of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) stand in support of this important Bill.

  • Ms He Ting Ru

    • Ms He Ting Ru said the shift to executive discretion should be founded in necessity.

      Verbatim
      Such a shift from a more rule-based model of data governance to one that relies more heavily on executive decision and ultimately, discretion, should be founded in necessity.

  • Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo

    • Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo said the offences carry fines of up to $5,000, imprisonment of up to two years, or both.

      Verbatim
      These offences carry the same penalties already set out in the PSGA, which are fines of up to $5,000, imprisonment of up to two years, or both.

Adjournment Motion on fire safety in homes Adjournment Motion12 January 2026 matter-adj-2777

An Adjournment Motion where a Non-Constituency Member spoke on fire safety in homes and the Minister of State for Home Affairs responded.

The Minister said the Land Transport and Related Matters Bill was introduced for First Reading, which makes it an offence to keep unsafe devices such as non-UL2272 certified e-scooters. He also said MOT targets legislative amendments later this year to strengthen regulations on online sale of AMDs. The record does not set out other practical impacts of the proposals raised.

  • Mr Low Wu Yang Andre

    • Fire fatalities rose from three in 2023 to five in 2024.

      Verbatim
      Fire fatalities rose from three in 2023 to five in 2024.

    • By August 2025, at least eight fire deaths had been recorded.

      Verbatim
      by August 2025, we had already recorded at least eight fire deaths.

    • Proposed making installation of new entrance gates with an interior thumb turn an "essential improvement" under the HIP scheme, fully subsidised and not optional.

      Verbatim
      we should make the installation of new entrance gates with an interior thumb turn an "essential improvement" under the HIP scheme, fully subsidised and not optional.

    • Proposed eliminating wrought iron gates with double cylinder locks as an option.

      Verbatim
      Wrought iron gates with double cylinder locks should also be eliminated as an option.

    • Proposed encouraging or mandating pre-installation by developers of gates with single cylinder thumb-turn locks.

      Verbatim
      we should encourage or even mandate that the pre-installation by developers of gates with single cylinder thumb-turn locks.

    • Proposed a phased replacement plan for legacy gates with double cylinder locks for estates not set to have an HIP exercise in the near future, prioritising older estates.

      Verbatim
      We should also develop a phased replacement plan for legacy gates with double cylinder locks for estates that are not set to have an HIP exercise in the near future, prioritising older estates.

    • Proposed incorporating risks of keyed gates, additional padlocks and sealed window grilles into public education campaigns on fire safety.

      Verbatim
      we should incorporate the risks of keyed gates, additional padlocks and sealed window grilles into public education campaigns on fire safety.

    • AMD fires rose 21.8% in 2024 to 67 cases while PMA fires saw a 120% spike.

      Verbatim
      Active mobility device (AMD) fires rose 21.8% in 2024 to 67 cases while personal mobility aid (PMA) fires saw a dramatic 120% spike.

    • Proposed pushing for battery swapping systems to be commonplace.

      Verbatim
      I think we should push for battery swapping systems to be commonplace

    • Proposed building public charging hubs for AMDs, perhaps co-located with EV chargers in HDB car parks.

      Verbatim
      I propose that we build public charging hubs for AMDs, perhaps co-located with electric vehicle (EV) chargers in HDB car parks.

    • Proposed implementing periodic inspections of AMDs, especially batteries, with enforced replacement timelines as batteries degrade and age.

      Verbatim
      I would suggest that we implement periodic inspections of AMDs, especially batteries, with enforced replacement timelines as batteries degrade and age.

    • Proposed considering "Fire Escape Viability" – presence of single-point egress or enclosed corridors – as one factor in Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme selection for flat redevelopment.

      Verbatim
      we should consider "Fire Escape Viability" – presence of single-point egress or enclosed corridors – as one factor in Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme selection for flat redevelopment.

    • Proposed further expanding the installation of Home Fire Alarm Devices (HFAD) to all older flats.

      Verbatim
      I propose that we further expand the installation of the Home Fire Alarm Devices (HFAD) to all older flats.

    • Proposed rolling out sprinkler systems in common areas of older blocks systematically, not just as pilots.

      Verbatim
      we should roll out sprinkler systems in common areas of older blocks systematically, and not just as pilots.

    • Proposed implementing more rigorous inspection regimes for fire-fighting infrastructure – wet risers, dry risers, booster pumps – with published compliance rates and mandatory remediation timelines.

      Verbatim
      we should implement more rigorous inspection regimes for fire-fighting infrastructure – wet risers, dry risers, booster pumps – with published compliance rates and mandatory remediation timelines.

    • Proposed supporting Town Councils with clearer enforcement mandates, and more monetary resources and support to maintain safety standards and keep fire safety infrastructure in good working order.

      Verbatim
      we should support our Town Councils with clearer enforcement mandates, and more monetary resources and support to maintain the safety standards and keep fire safety infrastructure in good working order.

  • Mr Goh Pei Ming

    • Corrected the fatality figure: six in the whole of 2025.

      Verbatim
      We had six in the whole of 2025.

    • Residential fire situation is stable over the past five years, with fatalities fewer than six on average per year.

      Verbatim

    • Top three causes of residential fires in Singapore have been unattended cooking fires, fires of electrical origin, and naked flames such as candles.

      Verbatim
      the top three causes of residential fires in Singapore have been unattended cooking fires, which account for about a third of cases, fires of electrical origin and those arising from naked flames, such as candles.

    • Fire compartmentalisation principle is effective.

      Verbatim
      this fire compartmentalisation principle is effective.

    • On locks, there is a trade-off with practicality, and security is something Singaporeans prioritise and value.

      Verbatim
      we often have to trade off practicality as well. In this regard, security is also something that I think Singaporeans will prioritise and value.

    • The Fire Code is periodically updated.

      Verbatim
      the Fire Code is periodically updated.

    • The introduction of more recent Fire Code provisions does not mean that older flats are unsafe.

      Verbatim
      the introduction of more recent Fire Code provisions does not mean that older flats are unsafe

    • Older point blocks require a single exit staircase as stipulated by the Fire Code then, and based on risk analysis this is wearable because there are only a few units per floor, so the number of evacuees is much reduced.

    • AMDs accounted for less than 5% of residential fires over the past five years, but more than 10% of fire-related injuries and 25% of fatalities.

      Verbatim

    • Between 2022 and 2025, more than 70% of AMD-related residential fires involved devices that were either not certified or tested to the relevant standards or had been illegally modified.

      Verbatim

    • In the last five years, LTA detected over 5,000 cases of non-compliant AMDs and took action against offenders including riders, owners and retailers.

      Verbatim
      In the last five years, LTA detected over 5,000 cases of non-compliant AMDs and took action against offenders including riders, owners and retailers.

    • The Ministry of Transport earlier today introduced the Land Transport and Related Matters Bill for the First Reading, which makes it an offence to keep unsafe devices such as non-UL2272 certified e-scooters.

      Verbatim
      the Ministry of Transport (MOT) earlier today, introduced the Land Transport and Related Matters Bill for the First Reading. This Bill makes it an offence to keep unsafe devices, such as non-UL2272 certified e-scooters.

    • MOT is looking to strengthen regulations on the online sale of AMDs and targets to make the necessary legislative amendments later this year.

      Verbatim
      MOT is also looking to strengthen regulations on the online sale of AMDs and targets to make the necessary legislative amendments later this year.

    • The Active Mobility Fire Safety Taskforce, co-chaired by LTA and SCDF, will continue to outreach to AMD owners under the Be Device-Safe programme.

      Verbatim
      the Active Mobility Fire Safety Taskforce, co-chaired by LTA and SCDF, will continue to outreach to AMD owners under the Be Device-Safe programme

  • Mr Speaker

    • The Sitting tomorrow will commence at 12.00 pm.

      Verbatim
      Pursuant to Standing Order 2(3)(a), I wish to inform hon Members that the Sitting tomorrow will commence at 12.00 pm.

What happens next The Land Transport and Related Matters Bill was introduced for First Reading; MOT targets legislative amendments later this year. Parliament adjourned; the next Sitting is tomorrow at 12.00 pm.

  • Lower Investment Returns Reported by Temasek Holdings and GIC

    Mr Saktiandi Supaat → Mr Jeffrey Siow
    Asked

    MPs asked whether GIC's and Temasek's investment returns are competitive against global benchmarks, whether they have underperformed expectations, how this affects the Net Investment Returns Contribution and CPF/SSGS obligations, and whether their mandates, risk frameworks or public reporting should change.

    Said back

    Read the transcript (12 turns)
    Asked Mr Saktiandi Supaat

    Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether the Government assesses that Temasek’s and GIC’s risk-adjusted returns relative to appropriate global benchmarks remain competitive; and (b) how their mandates should evolve to balance capital preservation with the need for higher real returns ahead.

    Response Mr Jeffrey Siow

    Thank you. My reply will also cover Question No 4 for written answer filed by Mr Ng Shi Xuan for today's Sitting. Mr Speaker, recent media reports have compared the performance of GIC and Temasek with that of other funds, including other sovereign wealth funds. Such comparisons are often done, but they should be interpreted in their proper context because different funds operate under different mandates and risk profiles. The Government assesses GIC and Temasek's performance primarily against their respective mandates and risk profiles, and not with other funds. Our focus has always been on long-term performance, rather than on short-term or year-to-year fluctuations. GIC is the Government's fund manager, and its mandate is to preserve and enhance the international purchasing power of the assets under its management. In recent years, GIC took pre-emptive measures to moderate its risk exposure, in anticipation of increased market volatility and heightened valuations. These measures were intended to keep portfolio risks within acceptable limits and to guard against the possibility of significant asset impairment in the event of a sharp market correction. But as equity markets have continued to remain elevated, these prudent de-risking measures resulted in some foregone returns. Any assessment of returns must, therefore, be considered alongside the risks that are taken to achieve them – a point that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim made, where he referred to the Sharpe ratio in his Parliamentary Question (PQ). GIC monitors a wide range of risk indicators, including and beyond the Sharpe ratio. In fact, GIC publishes both the returns and volatility or the risks associated with its portfolio in its annual report to provide a more complete picture. Ultimately, what is more important is the longer-term performance that is achieved within acceptable risk limits. On that basis, GIC has achieved a real return of 3.8% per annum over the past 20 years. This outcome reflects, in part, GIC’s active management, which enabled it to consistently add value to portfolio returns, preserve the international purchasing power of the assets under its management and deliver returns above global inflation. Temasek began as a holding company for the Government’s local assets. While Singapore-based Temasek Portfolio Companies (TPCs) continue to form a core part of its total portfolio, Temasek has progressively expanded its direct equity investments overseas – initially in Asia, and more recently, across global markets. Temasek operates mainly as an active, bottom-up investor. It does not operate against a conventional reference portfolio. Instead, it invests directly in companies in the geographies and domains where it has built deep capabilities, and where it sees long-term growth potential. Relative to GIC, Temasek therefore operates at the higher end of the risk spectrum. In recent years, Temasek’s performance was affected by the performance of the Chinese market, though this was mitigated by higher returns from its growing investments in Europe and the United States (US). Nonetheless, over the last 20-year period, Temasek has reported a Total Shareholder Return of 8% per annum in US dollar terms. Taken as a whole, the Government’s assessment is that the returns generated by GIC and Temasek are reasonable and within expectations, given their mandates and risk profiles. We will continue to review their mandates and performance regularly, in line with changes in the global economic investment landscape. Some Members asked about the implications of our investment entities’ recent performance on the sustainability of the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) and the Government’s ability to meet our Central Provident Fund (CPF) liabilities. As explained in this House previously, the Net Investment Return framework was designed to ensure a steady and sustainable stream of income for the annual Budget. The NIRC is thus derived from the expected long-term real rate …

    Supplementary questions from Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim, Mr Fadli Fawzi, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Shawn Loh (10 further turns)
    Mr Saktiandi SupaatThank you, Mr Speaker. I have two supplementary questions. First of all, I would like to declare that I am an employee of a financial institution. Global markets have become more volatile. In the previous PQ, we have actually discussed about expenditure on healthcare and others being more demanding. So, my two supplementary questions, Mr Speaker: first, how will the Ministry model the impact of a prolonged global resolve cycle on sovereign investment returns and the resulting implications for the Budget stability and social spending sustainability? My second supplementary question is whether the Government plans to enhance long-term public reporting on portfolio risks? I think the Acting Minister mentioned the Sharpe ratio and others as well. But in terms of public reporting on portfolio risks, volatility and drawdowns for Singapore's foreign investment entities to strengthen public confidence, as reliance on investment income increases?
    Mr Jeffrey SiowMr Speaker, I thank the hon Member for his supplementary questions. The Government's approach on assessing the returns of our investment entities is to take a long-term view. Market outcomes will inevitably fluctuate from year to year, there will be periods where returns are weak. But the way our system works is that these are not directly linked to our NIRC. The Government's strong balance sheet, as I explained earlier in my reply, enables it to take investment risks and ride out market cycles that are inherent in investing for the long term. We have a significant buffer on net assets, which enables the Government to guarantee CPF savings and pay fair interest rates on CPF savings despite changes in the financial cycle. And this is also why we are able to have a significant stream of investment income through the NIRC, which is then used to meet important spending priorities, as we discussed earlier. The Net Investment Returns taken into the Government Budget every year is based on the long-term expected returns of the investment entities, not on the year-to-year returns, which can fluctuate. In addition, the asset base that is used to calculate the NIRC is smoothed over the long …
    Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome LimThank you, Speaker. I have two supplementary questions, one on GIC and the other on Temasek.     Mr Jeffrey SiowThank you, Mr Speaker. As I mentioned in my reply earlier, the Government assesses the returns of our investment entities based on their mandates and risk profiles. And the second question is in regard to the fact that GIC and Temasek are active managers that have …
    Mr Jeffrey SiowThank you, Mr Speaker. I thank the hon Member for his questions. I agree with the hon Member that we should recognise that it has become more challenging to generate good investment returns in the current global environment and that this trend is likely to persist in the longer term. That is why the Government will continue to take a prudent approach in ensuring that our investment income is able to meet our long-term obligations. So, can I ask the Acting Minister, whether the Ministry of Finance sees investing more of our Reserves into the local infrastructures that comes with commercial returns, as another way to deploy our growing Reserves? And as such, we will have to assess for their difference in performance. For example, the holding company for the strategic companies that we hold, like Singapore …
    Mr Jeffrey SiowThank you, Mr Speaker. The hon Member asked two questions. Number one, I think is on whether or not, given the competition with global funds, whether Temasek or GIC should take a different focus and to focus on investment in local infrastructure – I think that was the first question. And the second question, was whether or not, given that it has a cluster, in terms of local Singapore companies, whether we should evaluate performance differently. I think in gist, those are the two questions. On the first question, I think we do not work on the basis of individual investment decisions. I think we want to structure how the relationship between the Government and our investment entities, structure them at the broad level to enable them to fulfil this mandate of achieving sustainable returns, preserving our asset base, while giving them, as commercial entities, the freedom to do the things that they need to do. And so, insofar as requiring them to have a specific investment focus or to invest locally, I think that is something as an entity, they need to decide and in light of the mandate that we have given them, to see whether that it is the most preferred strategy.   • Stepping Up Public Education Efforts in Light of Residential Unit Fires in 2025 and Review of Singapore’s Building, Fire and Construction Safety Codes

    Mr Ng Chee Meng → Mr Goh Pei Ming
    Asked

    Mr Ng Chee Meng asked how many residential unit fires there were in 2025 compared with 2024, and whether the Ministry will step up education, enforcement and inspections, especially in older housing estates. Mr Alex Yam asked, in light of the Tai Po fire in Hong Kong, whether Singapore's building, fire and construction safety codes will be reviewed for high-density developments and what further compliance and enforcement measures are being taken.

    Said back

    In 2025 there were 1,051 residential building fires, up from 968 in 2024, although fires as a share of total dwelling stock fell from 0.067% in 2021 to 0.065% in 2025. The Government has started reviewing early observations from Hong Kong's ongoing investigations and will announce the outcome of that review in due course. The Minister set out existing safeguards — the Fire Code, Town Council and MCST responsibility for common areas, SCDF aerial appliances reaching 90 metres, and refuge floors in buildings above 40 storeys — alongside community programmes such as Community Resilience Days and the Responders Plus Programme.

    • 1,051 residential building fires in 2025, up from 968 in 2024, described as a slight increase within a stable five-year trend.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • Fires as a share of total dwelling stock fell from 0.067% in 2021 to 0.065% in 2025.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • A review of early observations from Hong Kong's investigations is under way, with the outcome to be announced later.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • All buildings must be designed and built to the prevailing Fire Code.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • Town Councils and MCSTs manage common areas in HDB estates and strata-titled developments, including SCDF fire safety compliance.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • SCDF has aerial appliances reaching up to 90 metres and surveillance drones for high-rise operations.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • High-rise residential buildings above 40 storeys need at least one refuge floor per 20 storeys.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • SCDF responds to most fire and rescue incidents, including high-rise fires, within eight minutes.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • Structures above 24 metres (about eight storeys) must have fire lifts switchable to manual operation; additional fire lifts are required at 40 storeys and above.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • Construction hoarding must be non-combustible, fire safety systems must stay functional, and bamboo scaffolding is not allowed.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • SCDF runs about 16 Community Resilience Days a year, and more than 60,000 people joined the Responders Plus Programme between January 2024 and August 2025.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • Home Fire Alarm Devices are encouraged for seniors and subsidised under the Enhancement for Active Seniors Programme.Mr Goh Pei Ming
    • Unattended cooking is cited as the main primary cause of fires.Mr Goh Pei Ming

  • Temasek Holdings' Planned Restructuring and Potential Impact on Investment Performance and Returns

    Mr Ng Shi Xuan → Mr Jeffrey Siow
    Asked

    Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui asked whether the Government is aware of the mandates, workforce sizes and manpower cost benchmarks for each new entity after Temasek's planned 2026 restructuring, and whether the Ministry assessed workforce size and manpower costs against investment performance, risk management and organisational nimbleness.

    Said back

    Mr Jeffrey Siow said the Government's mandate for Temasek is to deliver good, sustainable long-term returns, and that the Government ensures a competent board but does not direct individual investment decisions. He said Temasek does not operate against a specific conventional reference portfolio, though it publishes indexes such as MSCI and STI as reference. He said there is no requirement for Temasek to pursue specific strategic or economic development strategies, and that restructuring is for the Temasek board to determine. The Government holds the board accountable for long-term returns on net portfolio performance after deducting all investment fees and expenses.

    • The Government's mandate for Temasek is to deliver good, sustainable long-term returns.Mr Jeffrey Siow
    • The Government ensures Temasek has a competent board but does not influence or direct individual investment decisions.Mr Jeffrey Siow
    • Temasek does not operate against a specific conventional reference portfolio, but publishes indexes such as MSCI and STI as reference.Mr Jeffrey Siow
    • There is no requirement for Temasek to pursue specific strategic or economic development strategies; such efforts are led by the Government.Mr Jeffrey Siow
    • Enterprise Singapore runs a Startup SG Equity scheme where the Government co-invests with third-party investors in Singapore-based deep tech startups.Mr Jeffrey Siow
    • The Government has co-invested with Temasek in the Local Enterprises Fund and the Anchor Fund, both managed commercially by 65 Equity Partners.Mr Jeffrey Siow
    • Restructuring decisions are for the Temasek board, and the Government does not intervene.Mr Jeffrey Siow
    • The Government holds Temasek's board accountable for long-term returns on net portfolio performance after deducting all investment fees and expenses.Mr Jeffrey Siow

    Supplementary questions Supplementary questions covered Temasek's assessment of Singapore-based companies, listed versus unlisted returns, government levers if returns are unsatisfactory, and the illiquidity premium.

    Left open in this exchange (3)

    Raised by the question and not addressed in the response. Recorded as open points, not as findings.

    • The specific mandates, workforce sizes and manpower cost benchmarks for each new entity after Temasek's planned 2026 restructuring.

    • Details of the planned 2026 restructuring and the new entities involved.

    Asked Mr Ng Shi Xuan

    Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether there are circumstances under which Temasek Holdings is expected to accept lower financial returns when pursuing strategic or developmental outcomes under the investment mandates given by the Government; and (b) if so, how are such expectations articulated and governed, given that the Government does not direct or influence individual investment decisions made by Temasek Holdings.

    Response Mr Jeffrey Siow

    My response will also cover Question No 3 for written answer filed for today's Sitting, as well as the question filed by Mr Kenneth Tiong for oral answer at a subsequent Sitting. I would thereafter invite Members who have filed questions for this and future Sittings to seek clarifications if need be. If sufficiently addressed, the Member may wish to withdraw the question filed for a subsequent Sitting.

    Supplementary questions from Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim, Mr Ng Shi Xuan (4 further turns)
    Mr Ng Shi XuanI thank the Acting Minister for his answer. I have three supplementary questions. The second one would be, over the past decade, have unlisted investments outperformed listed assets and what are the factors that can explain any such of these performance differences? The last one would be, I understand that the Government assesses that the long-term performance has been satisfactory, but it is a long-term view – and that is good in the sense that we do not take any knee-jerk reactions. But in the event that it is deemed unsatisfactory, what levers does the Government have to rectify or act on their returns and investment?
    Mr Jeffrey SiowMr Speaker, let me recap the three questions very quickly. Second is the performance of unlisted assets versus listed assets; how do we assess them? And then thirdly, how do we assess their short-term variations in performance and what do we do if that is affected? So, on the first question, I have answered that as part of the previous Parliamentary Question. I think, first of all, for Temasek, we do assess them overall, looking at their broad mandate, whether or not they have performed to meet the mandate in delivering sustainable long-term returns. At the same time, we do work with them closely to understand the performance of the different groups of companies. Looking at how the Singapore portfolio companies perform, we do work with them closely to understand if they have performed in a certain way and to see how the performance of those companies can be specifically improved, because these are Singaporean companies and they are important to us. So, we do work with them on that basis. But in terms of assessing them overall as …
    Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome LimMy understanding is that Temasek currently holds about half of its portfolio in public assets and the remainder in private exposures. That said, however, it appears to me that if we accept the state of affairs, Temasek is not successfully harvesting this illiquidity premium that, according to the Minister, it is trying to maximise according to its mandate. It really depends on the mandate and the risk profile that Temasek was set up to do. As I explained in my reply, Temasek is not quite the same as a typical sovereign wealth fund. It is an active bottom-up investor, and it also has a history and development as a holding company for Singapore portfolio companies. Nonetheless, as a comparison, I think Temasek's performance has, indeed, been commensurate with other sovereign wealth funds with a higher risk profile, such as the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board. Just as a comparison, both have achieved 20-year annualised total shareholder returns of about 8%. So, the Government does expect Temasek to achieve good sustainable returns over the long term.   • Animal Welfare Groups' Involvement in Trap-Neuter-Rehome/Release-Manage Programme

    Ms Lee Hui Ying → Mr Alvin Tan
    Asked Ms Lee Hui Ying

    Minister for National Development (a) whether the Ministry or Animal and Veterinary Service (AVS) works with Animal Welfare Groups (AWGs) on the operations of the Trap-Neuter-Rehome/Release-Manage programme; and (b) if so, whether consultations take place between the AWGs and AVS before every trapping operation.

    Response Mr Alvin Tan

    Mr Speaker, my answer will also address related questions for written answer by Ms Diana Pang and Mr Kenneth Tiong, scheduled for subsequent Sittings. Sir, since 2018, the Animal and Veterinary Service (AVS) has worked with its partners on the Trap-Neuter-Rehome/Release-Manage (TNRM) programme to manage the free-roaming dog population in Singapore. Our TNRM partners play key roles, including conducting trapping and sterilisation operations. Upon identification of an unsterilised free-roaming dog, AVS will work with the TNRM partner responsible for the designated area to commence trapping operations. In situations that present risk to public safety, AVS will intervene swiftly. For instance, in the case of the recent trapping operation at Seletar West Farmway 8 on 14 November 2025, AVS' animal management contractor was activated to trap and remove three free-roaming dogs, which were confirmed by several victims to have been involved in multiple chasing and biting incidents. The operation was carried out safely under the supervision of AVS staff and is in line with existing protocols under TNRM. This includes complying with the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) standards on Stray Dog Population Control to ensure that uncovered wire loops or ropes were not used during the trapping process and also giving due consideration to personnel and animal safety in determining the restraint procedures. AVS will continue to work closely with TNRM partners in the management of free-roaming dogs to safeguard both public safety and well-being of the dogs. AVS colleagues and I visited our partners last week to discuss ways we can better collaborate moving forward. For instance, we intend to review joint protocols and further improve communication and coordination. These build on existing collaboration channels, such as TNRM rehoming efforts, outreach and AVS-led adoption drives.

    Supplementary questions from Ms Lee Hui Ying (2 further turns)
    Ms Lee Hui YingThank you, Mr Speaker, and thank you, Minister of State for the comprehensive reply. I have two supplementary questions. First, what is the nature of such discussions with the different Animal Welfare Groups (AWGs) prior to, perhaps, trapping operations? Behind every animal held is a human and an AWG where they celebrate every rescue, recovery and adoption and feeling the grief when an animal suffers. The work is built on care, and it has not been easy. At the same time, I have also personally interacted with so many dedicated AVS and National Parks Board (NParks) officers, so I wanted to do a special thanks for their commitment for this constant work with the AWGs to rehome animals and balance the competing needs with care and professionalism. The second question really is then: can the Minister of State provide an assessment on the effectiveness of the TNRM programme so far? I am heartened to know that a review is due. So, what will this review entail and how will it be done? I hope and I urge AVS and NParks to continue working closely with the AWGs to further improve the TNRM methods.
    Mr Alvin TanSir, I thank the Member for her continued support for our TNRM efforts and also working very closely with the AWGs. Indeed, there is a lot of discussion and collaboration between AVS and the AWGs, and that is why we are also refining the TNRM protocols. That includes the management of free-roaming dogs, the review of various trapping measures and also, how to further improve coordination and collaboration between AVS and our TNRM partners. That also includes streamlining feedback channels and conducting regular stakeholder engagements and workshops. In fact, when I visited them on Friday, I encouraged them to join our TNRM workshop that is scheduled for 15 January, which is Thursday. I am very happy that many of our partners will be joining this TNRM workshop for us to continue to refine these processes. On the effectiveness of the TNRM programme, while Members might know that it started in 2018, we have thus far trapped 4,470 dogs, rehomed 2,048 dogs and sterilised 80% of the free-roaming dog population. That is above our target of 70% and that has resulted in a reduction of 80% of feedback cases. So, we will continue to continue to work with our TNRM partners to further refine …

  • Lessons from Hong Kong's High-rise Fire for Singapore's Review of Building (Strata Management) Act

    Mr Fadli Fawzi → Ms Sun Xueling
    Asked Mr Fadli Fawzi

    Minister for National Development (a) whether the Government's review of the Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act 2004 will incorporate learnings from the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po, Hong Kong; and (b) if not, why not.

    Response Ms Sun Xueling

    The Hong Kong authorities are still investigating the Wang Fuk Court fire incident. Notwithstanding, the Government has been reviewing the learning points based on the early observations. Where relevant, the Ministry of National Development will incorporate findings from the review into our legislative and policy framework, including the Building (Strata Management) Act.

    Supplementary questions from Mr Fadli Fawzi (2 further turns)
    Mr Fadli FawziThank you, Speaker. Given that one of the potential causes of the fire that the Hong Kong government is looking into was the corruption by the management of the Wang Fuk Court, will the Ministry or the Building and Construction Authority be looking into how to strengthen oversight over management councils that are conducting large-scale infrastructure repairs, whether by the Government or by the subsidiary proprietors themselves?
    Ms Sun XuelingI thank the Member for his question. When reviewing the Building (Strata Management) Act, we will be looking at the powers of the Management Corporation Strata Title. I will be sharing more information in due course.
